title: A shared lunch
hook: lunch as a small langar: share something
tomorrow: why does the evening prayer open with a morning question?

segments.voice: Last week ended at work: the Name in the mouth, the hands on the job. Remember at work. Now it's lunchtime.

The coins are already in his hand. His father's instructions are simple: go to the market, make a good deal, a true bargain. The young Nanak sets out, and on the road he meets a group of holy men who have gone hungry. He looks at the money. He looks at them. He spends every coin on food, and he comes home with nothing to sell and nothing to show. His father is furious. And Nanak's answer, in the story Sikhs tell, is that he did exactly what he was asked.
screen: `COINS IN HAND: MAKE A TRUE BARGAIN.` → `HUNGRY MEN ON THE ROAD.` → `HOME WITH NOTHING.`

segments.voice: Feeding the hungry was the true bargain, sacha sauda. The story comes from the janamsakhis, the life stories of Guru Nanak, and it points at something the Gurus built into Sikh life: langar, the shared kitchen. In a gurdwara, everyone sits on the floor in a row, the pangat, and eats the same food, whoever they are. Tradition says the third Guru asked visitors to eat in the pangat before they came to see him. And Guru Nanak says it in the Granth, on ang 1245, in paraphrase: the one who earns by honest work and gives some of it away, Nanak, recognizes the path. Sikhs have a phrase for that last part: vand chhako, share and eat. Not leftovers after you've had enough. A share set aside before. So a lunch can be a small langar. Half a sandwich across the table, a second fork, a box of samosas opened in the break room instead of eaten in the car. The bargain isn't about how much. It's whether the plate is yours, or the table's.
screen: `SACHA SAUDA: THE TRUE BARGAIN.` · `LANGAR: ONE ROW, ONE MEAL.` · `ANG 1245: EARN, AND GIVE SOME.` · `LUNCH AS A SMALL LANGAR.` · then, large: `SHARE THE PLATE.`

segments.voice: Think of your next meal, and decide now which part of it goes to someone else, and to whom. Say that person's name once, quietly. Then sit, and let the decision settle before the food arrives.
A shared lunch. A meal with a share set aside first: a small langar, wherever you eat.
Your line: share the plate. Nanak spent every coin and called it a good deal. Enjoy lunch.

howItsDone: Gurdwaras serve langar, a free shared meal, to everyone who comes, seated together in the pangat; Sikhs speak of vand chhako, sharing what you have, and some carry it into ordinary meals at home, school and work.
